title: Flash-flood low spots vs USGS high-water marks (Hurricane Ida, NYC, Sept 1 2021)
question: Can a terrain-only analysis (low spots where rain water collects) find the places that flooded during Ida, and how deep it got?

hwm.about: USGS high-water marks, NYC five boroughs, Ida 2021 (doi:10.5066/P9OMBJPQ)

hwm_dictionary.about: Data dictionary for the high-water marks

assumptions: Water collects in terrain low spots (sinks) of the bare-earth surface; storm sewers, buildings and curbs are ignored.
A mark's flood depth is its height above ground, from the USGS survey.
Places that did not flood are unknown; random points near the marks stand in for them.

traps.check: The CSV's first line is a citation, not the header. Parsing from line 1 silently mislabels every column.
Mark elevations and depths are in feet; 3DEP elevation is in meters. Mixing them inflates or shrinks depths 3.28x.
Marks exist only where it flooded, so they cannot measure false alarms. A fair test compares marks with control points.
Some marks were surveyed inside buildings or basements, where depth is measured from an interior floor. They must be flagged, not mixed with street marks.
The DEM is bare earth: sewers, buildings and curbs are missing, so the model can't capture flooding from sewer backups.

interior_reviewed.method: Read each mark's USGS location description and notes; flagged when the water line was measured inside a building (basement wall or hallway, inside a door). 41147 was transposed from the inside of a garage door to an outdoor pad and is kept as interior. Exterior walls and garage entrances are not interior. Verify with photos in the USGS Flood Event Viewer.
interior_reviewed.replaces: A keyword rule (basement|inside|garage|...) that flagged 31 marks, including exterior garage doors and a playground wheel (found by the agent evaluation, tasks T14 and T16).
